stem: When you buy one share of a company's stock, what have you actually bought?
options: A loan to the company that it must repay to you with interest
A small piece of ownership in the company
A promise that the company will buy the share back from you at a set price
A fixed yearly payment that the company guarantees
explanation: Stock is equity: a slice of ownership with a residual claim, and dividends are never guaranteed. A loan repaid with interest describes a bond, not a share. (02-foundations.md §3.A.1, §3.A.3)

stem: A share you bought for $40 is now worth $50. By what percentage has its price increased?
explanation: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old = (50 − 40) ÷ 40 = 25%. Dividing by the new price ($10 ÷ $50 = 20%) is the classic asymmetry error. (02-foundations.md §3.J.1)

stem: You own a bond that pays $40 a year on every $1,000 invested. Newly issued bonds of the same quality now pay $60 a year per $1,000. If you want to sell your bond today, what must happen?
options: You must accept less than $1,000, so the buyer's return catches up to what new bonds pay
You can ask for more than $1,000, because your bond is older and proven
You will get exactly $1,000, because the bond's face value never changes
You cannot sell it until it matures
explanation: Nobody pays full price for $40 a year when $60 a year is available, so the price of the existing bond drops until its yield matches the market — the price/yield seesaw. Face value is what the issuer repays at maturity, not what a buyer pays today. (02-foundations.md §3.H.4, §3.G.3)

stem: You put $1,000 in an account that pays 10% interest once a year, and the interest is left in the account to earn interest itself. How much is in the account after two years?
explanation: Compounding: $1,000 × 1.10 × 1.10 = $1,210 — the second year's 10% is earned on $1,100, not $1,000. $1,200 is simple interest (interest on principal only). (02-foundations.md §3.G.2)

stem: Your savings account pays 2% a year. Over the same year, the prices of the things you buy rise by 3%. What happens to what your savings can buy?
options: It grows, because the account balance is larger than a year ago
It shrinks, because prices rose faster than the balance grew
It stays the same, because the interest offsets the price increases
It shrinks by exactly 3%, because interest does not count against inflation
explanation: Real return = nominal rate − inflation = 2% − 3% = about −1%, so purchasing power falls even though the dollar balance rose. The interest does count; it just does not fully offset the 3% price rise. (02-foundations.md §3.F.2)

stem: An investor buys 100 shares of XYZ common stock on the New York Stock Exchange. Who receives the money the investor pays?
options: XYZ Corporation, the issuer of the shares
The New York Stock Exchange
Another investor who sold the shares
The underwriter that originally brought XYZ public
explanation: An exchange trade is a secondary-market transaction: investors trade with each other and the issuer receives nothing. The issuer is paid only in the primary market (an IPO or follow-on offering). (02-foundations.md §3.B.2)

stem: A broker-dealer fills a customer's buy order by selling shares out of its own inventory. In this trade the firm is compensated by:
options: A markup built into the price the customer pays
A commission disclosed separately on the confirmation
A commission plus a markup on the same trade
A management fee based on the customer's assets
explanation: Selling from inventory is acting as a dealer (principal), which is compensated by a markup; a commission is the broker (agent) capacity. A firm may not charge both on a single trade. (02-foundations.md §3.C.1)

stem: Which of the following is protected by FDIC insurance?
options: Shares of a stock mutual fund purchased at a bank branch
Common stock held in a brokerage account
A variable annuity sold by a bank's registered representative
A 12-month certificate of deposit issued by an FDIC-member bank
explanation: FDIC insures bank deposits (checking, savings, CDs) up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. It never covers securities — mutual funds, stocks or annuities — even when bought at a bank, which is why the 'not FDIC insured / may lose value' disclosure is required. (02-foundations.md §3.D.7)

stem: A customer buys shares of a listed common stock in a regular-way transaction. When does the trade settle?
options: The same business day as the trade
One business day after the trade date
Two business days after the trade date
Three business days after the trade date
explanation: Since 2024-05-28, regular-way settlement for stocks, corporate and municipal bonds, ETFs and listed options is T+1 under amended SEC Rule 15c6-1. T+2 is the pre-2024 cycle still found in stale prep material; same-day is cash settlement. (02-foundations.md §3.E step 7)

stem: Which of the following risks CANNOT be reduced by diversifying a stock portfolio across many issuers and industries?
options: Business risk
Credit risk
Market risk
Liquidity risk
explanation: Market risk is systematic: it affects the whole market at once and cannot be diversified away (it is measured by beta). Business, credit and liquidity risks are issuer-specific, non-systematic risks that diversification reduces. (02-foundations.md §3.H.2, §3.H.3)

stem: A FINRA member broker-dealer violates an MSRB rule while selling municipal bonds. Which body is responsible for enforcing that rule against the firm?
options: The MSRB
FINRA
The state securities administrator
The municipal issuer
explanation: The MSRB writes rules for municipal dealers but has no enforcement arm; FINRA enforces MSRB rules against broker-dealers (bank regulators do so for bank dealers). The MSRB cannot regulate issuers at all (Tower Amendment). (02-foundations.md §3.D.3)

stem: A corporate bond with a 6% coupon is trading at $1,200. What is its current yield?
explanation: Current yield = annual interest ÷ market price = $60 ÷ $1,200 = 5.0%. 6% is the nominal (coupon) yield, which never changes; 7.5% would be the current yield if the bond traded at $800. (02-foundations.md §3.J.4)

stem: The Federal Open Market Committee directs the sale of Treasury securities in the open market. Which of the following is the MOST likely result?
options: Bank reserves increase and short-term interest rates fall
The money supply expands and bond prices rise
Bank reserves increase and bond prices fall
The money supply contracts and bond prices fall
explanation: When the Fed sells securities it drains reserves from the banking system (tight money): money supply down, interest rates up, and therefore bond prices down. Buying securities produces the opposite chain. (02-foundations.md §3.F.6; 09-regulation-trading-economics.md §3.14)

stem: A corporate bond is quoted at 98 3/8. What is its dollar price?
explanation: Corporate and municipal bonds are quoted as a percent of $1,000 par in eighths: 3/8 = 0.375, so 98.375% × $1,000 = $983.75. Reading the fraction as a decimal ($983.38) is the standard error. (02-foundations.md §3.J.3)

stem: A company reports current assets of $600,000, which include inventory of $150,000, and current liabilities of $300,000. What is its quick (acid-test) ratio?
explanation: Quick ratio = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities = ($600,000 − $150,000) ÷ $300,000 = 1.5. 2.0 is the current ratio, which leaves inventory in. (02-foundations.md §3.I.4)

stem: A Treasury note is quoted at 98.16 in the morning and 99.04 at the close. By how many dollars did the price of one $1,000 note change?
explanation: Treasury notes and bonds are quoted in 32nds: 98.16 = 98 16/32 = 98.5% = $985.00 and 99.04 = 99 4/32 = 99.125% = $991.25, a change of $6.25. Treating the quotes as decimals gives the $8.80 distractor. (02-foundations.md §3.J.3)

stem: All of the following are considered leading economic indicators EXCEPT:
options: Average weekly initial claims for unemployment insurance
New building permits for private housing
Stock prices as measured by the S&P 500
Average duration of unemployment
explanation: Initial jobless claims, building permits and stock prices all turn before the economy and are on the Conference Board's leading index; the average duration of unemployment is a lagging indicator. The trap is that jobless claims lead while unemployment measures lag. (02-foundations.md §3.F.5; 09-regulation-trading-economics.md §3.14)

stem: A customer holds $600,000 of securities and $200,000 of cash in an individual account, and $300,000 of securities in a joint account with her spouse, all at the same broker-dealer. The firm fails and is liquidated under SIPC. What is the MAXIMUM amount SIPC will cover for this customer?
explanation: SIPC covers $500,000 per separate customer capacity, of which up to $250,000 may be cash. The individual account ($800,000 claim, $200,000 cash) is capped at $500,000; the joint account is a separate capacity and its $300,000 is fully covered, for $800,000 total. (02-foundations.md §3.D.6)

stem: A corporation reports net income of $8,000,000, pays $800,000 in preferred dividends, and has 3,000,000 common shares outstanding. Its common stock trades at $36. What is the stock's price-to-earnings ratio?
explanation: EPS = (net income − preferred dividends) ÷ common shares = ($8,000,000 − $800,000) ÷ 3,000,000 = $2.40, and P/E = $36 ÷ $2.40 = 15. Forgetting to subtract the preferred dividends gives EPS of $2.67 and the 13.5 distractor. (02-foundations.md §3.I.7)

stem: A customer buys 200 shares of a listed stock in a cash account on Thursday, August 20, 2026. Under Regulation T, what is the last day the customer may pay for the purchase without the firm requesting an extension?
options: Friday, August 21
Monday, August 24
Tuesday, August 25
Wednesday, August 26
explanation: Regular-way settlement is T+1 (Friday, August 21), and Reg T's payment period is settlement plus two business days, so payment is due Tuesday, August 25 (T+3). Wednesday reflects the pre-2024 T+2 cycle plus two days (T+4), which is now stale. (02-foundations.md §3.E step 7)

stem: A company that completed its IPO three years ago files a registration statement and sells 2,000,000 newly issued common shares to the public through an underwriting syndicate. Which statement about this transaction is TRUE?
options: It is a secondary market transaction because the company is already publicly traded
It is a secondary distribution because the shares are sold after the initial public offering
It is a fourth market transaction if the shares are placed with institutional investors
It is a primary market transaction because the issuer receives the proceeds
explanation: Follow the cash: whenever the issuer sells new shares and receives the money it is a primary-market transaction, even though the industry calls it a 'secondary offering.' A secondary distribution is a sale of existing shares by insiders, where the issuer gets nothing. (02-foundations.md §3.B.1)

stem: All of the following statements about a zero-coupon bond are TRUE EXCEPT:
options: Its holder faces substantial reinvestment risk on the periodic interest payments
It is sold at a deep discount and redeemed at par at maturity
It carries greater interest-rate risk than a coupon bond of the same maturity
Its rate of return is locked in at purchase if it is held to maturity
explanation: A zero pays no periodic interest, so there is nothing to reinvest and it has no reinvestment risk — that is precisely why its return is locked in when held to maturity. The trade-off is maximum interest-rate (price) risk, since all of its value is one distant payment. (02-foundations.md §3.H.5)

stem: Which of the following interest rates is set directly by the Federal Reserve rather than determined by banks or the market?
options: The federal funds rate
The discount rate
The prime rate
The broker call loan rate
explanation: The Fed Board sets the discount rate it charges banks at the discount window. The fed funds rate is charged bank-to-bank and moves daily within a target range the FOMC sets — the Fed targets it but does not set it — while prime and broker call rates are set by commercial banks. (02-foundations.md §3.F.1, §4 trap 7)

stem: Which of the following corporate transactions would have NO effect on the company's working capital?
options: Declaring and paying a cash dividend to common stockholders
Issuing 20-year bonds for cash
Collecting an account receivable in cash
Purchasing a machine for cash
explanation: Collecting a receivable swaps one current asset (receivables) for another (cash), so working capital (current assets − current liabilities) is unchanged. Declaring and paying a dividend or buying equipment with cash reduces it; issuing long-term bonds for cash raises it, because the new liability is long-term. (02-foundations.md §3.I.4, §4 trap 10)

stem: A corporation declares a regular quarterly cash dividend with a record date of Thursday, June 11, 2026. What is the LAST day an investor can buy the stock in a regular-way trade and still receive the dividend?
options: Tuesday, June 9
Thursday, June 11
Friday, June 12
Wednesday, June 10
explanation: Under T+1 (FINRA Rule 11140 as amended 2024-05-28) the ex-dividend date for a regular cash dividend is the record date itself, so a purchase on Wednesday, June 10 settles on the record date and earns the dividend; buying on June 11 is ex-dividend. Tuesday, June 9 is the stale T+2-era answer ('ex-date one business day before record'). (02-foundations.md §3.E step 8)
